extracted.intended_audience: citizens and voters (specifically the people of New York) debating ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the constitutional design and practical sufficiency of the House of Representatives: number, apportionment, qualifications, informational needs, and institutional safeguards that secure fidelity to constituents. Focuses on why proposed sizes, election frequency, and structural rules will preserve republican liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative number and apportionment (one per 30,000)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of representatives is temporary at the outset (sixty-five) and may be augmented to one for every thirty thousand inhabitants as provided by the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains timetable (first census within three years, then every ten years) and reasons why the ratio (one per 30,000) will render the House a 'safe and competent guardian' of interests as population grows; gives numerical projections (e.g., ~100 after first census, 200 after 25 years, 400 after 50 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional mechanisms for periodic reapportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Decennial censuses and apportioned augmentations are required to adjust representation over time, with the single exception that each State shall have at least one representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the constitutional design: temporary initial number, three-year term before first census, repeated decennial censuses to 'readjust' apportionment and increase total representatives up to the limit of one per 30,000; argues this is comparable or superior to many State constitutions' protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary smallness is acceptable given Republican safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: A temporarily small House (e.g., 65 initially) is not dangerous to liberty because of the present character of the American people and checks from State legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from political character ('the present genius of the people of America') and the watchful motives and means of State legislatures to detect/defeat conspiracies; uses historical example of the Revolutionary Congress to show small bodies need not betray trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent elections ensure accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Short terms and frequent elections (representatives chosen every two years) are a primary restraint preserving representatives' responsibility to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains multiple psychological and political effects: 'temporary affection' to constituents, pride and vanity, self-interest in keeping favor, and the constant anticipation of review which prevent degeneracy; frequent elections are listed as 'the most effectual' precaution in republican government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineligibility to civil office during term prevents patronage corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of Congress are ineligible to any civil offices created, or whose emoluments are increased, during their term of election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constitutional bar limits the President/Senate's capacity to corrupt the House by promising offices; only ordinary-casualty vacancies could be used for appointments, which are unlikely to be sufficient to 'purchase the guardians of the people.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives need knowledge only of matters within federal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A representative's acquaintance with constituents' interests must extend only to those circumstances and interests 'to which the authority and care of the representative relate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits informational requirements to federal objects (commerce, taxation, militia). Argues ignorance of minute local matters unrelated to federal legislation is consistent with competent representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of State laws and state-legislative experience to supply local knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal representatives can obtain necessary local information via existing State laws and by drawing on experience as (or service in) State legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that state codes and proceedings provide preparatory labor and that many federal representatives will have been members of their State legislatures, enabling transmission of local knowledge to federal councils; a 'skillful individual in his closet with all the local codes' could compile laws for the union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain federal matters (commerce, taxation, militia) do not require extensive minute local knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce, duties connected to commerce, and militia regulation are largely susceptible to general rules or to synthesis from State laws, so a moderate number of representatives can legislate adequately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commerce requires information but much of it concerns state laws which representatives can use; taxation often involves duties related to commerce or simple internal collections preferred for uniformity; militia concerns general principles (terrain, organization) rather than fine local detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-to-population ratio is defensible by comparison (British House of Commons)
rubrics_metrics.description: A representative for every thirty thousand inhabitants is sufficient, supported by comparison to Britain where representation ratios and defects do not primarily arise from ignorance of the people's circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites British numbers (eight million people, 558 Commons members) and points out even with structural defects Britain retained valuable freedoms; uses comparative arithmetic to argue one per 30,000 will be adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larger electorates (diffusive election) do not elevate oligarchy; they likely pick fitter representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Electing representatives by larger bodies (five or six thousand voters) is not likely to produce rulers less sympathetic to the people than smaller electorates; in fact it may produce better choices and be less susceptible to intrigue/bribery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares state districts (some as large as those proposed for federal districts) and gives examples (New Hampshire senatorial districts, Massachusetts, New York, Pennsylvania) showing large-electorate selections have not produced oligarchic results; questions the reasonableness of preferring very small electorates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawmakers being subject to the laws they make restrains oppressive legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because representatives can make no law that will not operate on themselves and their friends, this creates a strong bond connecting rulers and people and helps prevent legal discriminations favoring the few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes this as 'one of the strongest bonds' tying rulers to the people; if the public spirit were debased to tolerate laws not applicable to legislators, that would indicate tolerance for anything but liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional leverage (House holds the purse) as a constitutional safeguard to obtain reapportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: The House's exclusive origination of money bills and control of supplies ('holds the purse') gives it an effective weapon to obtain redress and to secure augmentations and reapportionments when justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues this lever, combined with the bicameral structure (representation of citizens vs. representation of states), assures larger States and their representatives practical means to press for augmentations even if smaller states or the Senate resist; coalition dynamics and growth of new states further aid this.

rubrics_metrics.name: No qualifications of wealth, birth, religion, or profession to limit eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution permits no qualification of wealth, birth, religious faith, or civil profession to fetter eligibility for representatives; electors are 'the great body of the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to rebut the charge that the federal House would be taken from a class unsympathetic to the mass; this universal eligibility is presented as intrinsic to republican government and essential to preventing oligarchy.
